be after.verb type: **stative** — copular *be* plus a preposition, naming a state of pursuit, not an act. It rejects the progressive: ✗ *she is being after my job*.
be after.passive: **no** — *be* has no passive of its own, so the prepositional passive is impossible: ✗ *my job is been after by her*, ✗ *he was been after by the marshals*.

be along.verb type: **stative** in form — the copula plus a particle, so no progressive (✗ *the doctor is being along*) — though what it reports is an arrival, which is why it lives in the future: *will be along*, *should be along*.
be along.passive: **no** — there is no object, and *be* cannot be passivized in any case: ✗ *she was been along*.

be around.verb type: **stative** in all three senses — presence (*I'll be around*), long existence (*that diner has been around since the fifties*), and worldliness (*he has been around*). None of them takes the progressive: ✗ *he is being around*.
be around.passive: **no** — objectless and built on *be*: ✗ *the fifties have been been around since*.

be down.verb type: **stative** — a condition, whether it is mood (*she has been down*), a dead server (*the network is down*), or a number (*sales are down nine percent*). ✗ *the network is being down*.
be down.passive: **no** — no object anywhere in the entry, so nothing can be promoted: ✗ *the network was been down*.

be down with.verb type: **stative** — both the illness sense (*half the office is down with the flu*) and the slang approval sense (*I'm down with that*) name a state. ✗ *he is being down with the flu*.
be down with.passive: **no** — *be* takes no passive, so the object of *with* stays put: ✗ *the flu is been down with by half the office*.

be in.verb type: **stative** — presence (*the doctor is in*), fashion (*wide lapels are in*), participation (*I'm in*), and arrival of results (*the votes are in*) are all states. ✗ *the doctor is being in*.
be in.passive: **no** — intransitive throughout, and the copula has no passive: ✗ *the votes were been in*.

be in for.verb type: **stative** — it reports what is in store for someone, not anything the subject does: *we are in for a rough winter*. ✗ *we are being in for a rough winter*.
be in for.passive: **no** — the object of *for* cannot move to subject: ✗ *a surprise is been in for by him*.

be in on.verb type: **stative** — being one of the people who know or take part is a standing condition: *she has been in on the planning since the first week*. ✗ *she is being in on it*.
be in on.passive: **no** — built on *be*, so no passive at all: ✗ *the joke was been in on by everybody*.

be into.verb type: **stative** — a state of interest or attraction, whether the object is a hobby (*he is into synthesizers*) or a person (*she is into him*). ✗ *he is being into synthesizers*.
be into.passive: **no** — ✗ *synthesizers are been into by him*. The copula blocks it, however transitive the phrase looks.

be off.verb type: **stative** in senses 2 to 6 — canceled (*the wedding is off*), switched off, inaccurate, on leave, spoiled. Sense 1 (*I'm off*, *he was off before dawn*) reports a departure but still takes plain *be*: ✗ *I am being off*.
be off.passive: **no** — no object in any sense, and no passive of *be*: ✗ *the wedding was been off*.

be on.verb type: **stative** — happening (*the game is on*), switched on, showing, or taking a drug are all states, as are the fixed *it's on me* and *you're on*. ✗ *the game is being on*.
be on.passive: **no** — objectless and copular: ✗ *the game was been on*. Even sense 4, *she is on lithium*, cannot invert.

be on to.verb type: **stative** — a state of knowledge: having seen through someone (*the cops are on to him*) or having a promising lead (*you might be on to something*). ✗ *they are being on to him*.
be on to.passive: **no** — ✗ *he is been on to by the cops*. Compare the ordinary verb *suspect*, which does passivize.

be out.verb type: **stative** across all seven senses — absent, published, unfashionable, extinguished, ruled out, openly gay, unconscious. Each is a resulting condition, never an act: ✗ *the fire is being out*.
be out.passive: **no** — nothing to promote, and *be* has no passive: ✗ *the book was been out in March*.

be out of.verb type: **stative** — having none of something left is a state of the subject, not an event: *the store has been out of that model since June*. ✗ *we are being out of milk*.
be out of.passive: **no** — ✗ *milk is been out of by us*. The thing you have run out of can never become the subject.

be over.verb type: **stative** in both senses — an end reached (*the meeting is over*) and an attachment given up (*she is over him*). ✗ *the meeting is being over*, ✗ *she is being over him*.
be over.passive: **no** — sense 1 has no object, and sense 2's object resists promotion: ✗ *he is been over by her*.

be through.verb type: **stative** — a state of completion (*I'm through with the report*) or of a relationship finally ended (*we're through*). ✗ *I am being through with it*.
be through.passive: **no** — ✗ *the report is been through with*. What you are finished with stays inside the *with*-phrase.

be up.verb type: **stative** — awake (*she's up*), expired (*time is up*), afoot (*what's up*), higher (*sales are up*), running (*the site is up again*). All conditions: ✗ *the site is being up*.
be up.passive: **no** — intransitive and copular: ✗ *the lease was been up in March*.

be up for.verb type: **stative** — willingness (*are you up for a hike*), candidacy (*the contract is up for renewal*), or standing trial (*he's up for burglary*). ✗ *I am being up for it*.
be up for.passive: **no** — ✗ *a hike is been up for by me*. The renewal sense already reads passively in meaning, but the form cannot change.

be up to.verb type: **stative** — even sense 1, which describes activity, uses plain *be*: *what are you up to?*, never ✗ *what are you being up to?* Senses 2 and 3 (capability, responsibility) are plainly states.
be up to.passive: **no** — ✗ *something is been up to by him*; ✗ *the decision is been up to her*.

bear down.verb type: **action** — dynamic in all three senses: pressing harder on a pen, pushing in labor, redoubling effort. The progressive is normal: *she was bearing down on the last mile*.
bear down.passive: **no** — intransitive; whatever takes the pressure appears only after *on* (see *bear down on*): ✗ *the pedal was borne down*.

bear down on.verb type: **action** — dynamic throughout: a storm closing the distance, a hand pressing on a surface, regulators applying pressure. Progressive is the usual form: *the truck was bearing down on us*.
bear down on.passive: **restricted** — the prepositional passive works in the pressure sense (*the department has been borne down on by regulators all year*) but sounds forced with weather or traffic: ✗ *we were borne down on by the storm*.

bear on.verb type: **stative** — it states a relation of relevance, not an event: *two facts bear on the decision*. The progressive is out: ✗ *these findings are bearing on the case*.
bear on.passive: **no** — stative relations resist the prepositional passive: ✗ *the question is borne on by none of that*, ✗ *the timeline was borne upon by the memo*.

bear out.verb type: **action** with a stative flavor — it names the confirming, so the perfect is common (*every audit has borne out her account*) but the progressive is odd: ✗ *the data are bearing out his claim*.
bear out.passive: **yes**, and it is frequent — *her account was borne out by every audit since*, *his story wasn't borne out by anything in the log*. Note the participle *borne*, not ✗ *born*.

bear up.verb type: **action** — dynamic and durative, describing someone holding out under strain, so the progressive is idiomatic: *she is bearing up better than anyone expected*.
bear up.passive: **no** — intransitive; the strain follows *under* and cannot be promoted: ✗ *the traffic was borne up under by the bridge*.

bear with.verb type: **action** — dynamic, describing patience extended over a stretch of time: *thanks for bearing with us during the remodel*. Most often an imperative appeal, *bear with me*.
bear with.passive: **no** — the object of *with* stays put: ✗ *we were borne with by the customers*, ✗ *his complaints were borne with by her* (the plain transitive *bore* works instead).

beat back.verb type: **action** — dynamic and resultative: an attack or a fire is driven back to somewhere it was not. Progressive is fine: *crews were beating back the flames all night*.
beat back.passive: **yes** — *the flames were beaten back by dawn*, *the amendment was beaten back in committee*.

beat down.verb type: **action** in every sense — the sun coming down hard (sense 1), forcing a door, bargaining a price lower, breaking someone's spirit. Progressive throughout: *the sun was beating down*.
beat down.passive: **yes** in senses 2 to 4 — *the door had been beaten down*, *the price was beaten down to nine hundred*, *he was beaten down by two years of it*. **No** passive of sense 1: ✗ *we were beaten down on by the sun*.

beat off.verb type: **action** — dynamic in both: driving back an attack or a rival (sense 1) and the vulgar slang sense 2, which describes an act, not a state.
beat off.passive: **yes** in sense 1 — *the assault was beaten off with heavy losses*, *the takeover bid was beaten off*. **No** in sense 2, which takes no object: ✗ *it was beaten off by him*.

beat out.verb type: **action** — dynamic and telic in all four senses: edging out a rival, smothering a fire, tapping a rhythm, reaching base ahead of the throw.
beat out.passive: **yes** — *she was beaten out by a candidate with more experience*, *the fire was beaten out with a coat*, *the rhythm was beaten out on the tailgate*.

beat up.verb type: **action** — dynamic in senses 1 and 2 (assault; the reflexive *beat yourself up*). Sense 3 is no longer a verb at all but the attributive adjective *beat-up*: *a beat-up Corolla*.
beat up.passive: **yes** in sense 1 — *he was beaten up outside the bar*. **No** passive of the reflexive sense 2: ✗ *himself was beaten up by him* — say *he beat himself up over it*.

beat up on.verb type: **action** — dynamic, and typically iterative, which is why the progressive is so common: *the columnists have been beating up on the mayor all week*.
beat up on.passive: **restricted** — natural enough in the criticism sense (*the mayor has been beaten up on all week*), stiff with an agent: ✗ *your brother was beaten up on by you*.

become of.verb type: **stative** — it reports a fate, and only inside a *what/whatever* question: *whatever became of the couple upstairs?* No progressive: ✗ *what is becoming of the blueprints?*
become of.passive: **no** — *become* has no passive in any of its uses, this one included: ✗ *the shop was become of*, ✗ *the keys were become of by nobody*.

begin with.verb type: **action** in sense 1 — dynamic and inceptive: *begin with the basics*, *the book begins with a funeral*. Sense 2, *to begin with*, is a frozen adverbial, not a verb phrase you can inflect.
begin with.passive: **restricted** — the passive belongs to *begin* plus its own object, not to *begin with*: *the meeting was begun with a moment of silence* (formal) is fine, but ✗ *the basics were begun with*.

bend over backward.verb type: **action** — dynamic and idiomatic, describing effort made: *they bent over backward to accommodate us*. The progressive is normal: *he is bending over backward for these people*.
bend over backward.passive: **no** — the idiom takes no object at all; the person helped sits behind *for*: ✗ *we were bent over backward for by them*.

bet against.verb type: **action** — dynamic, whether the money is real (*bet against the Yankees*) or the sense is figurative (*never bet against her*).
bet against.passive: **restricted** — financial writing allows it (*the housing market was heavily bet against in 2007*), but ordinary speech does not: ✗ *she was bet against by nobody* — say *nobody bet against her*.

bet on.verb type: **action** — dynamic in sense 1 (wagering) and sense 2 (counting on something). Sense 3, *you can bet on it*, is a frozen promise and does not inflect freely.
bet on.passive: **restricted** — the literal wager passivizes stiffly: *the gray horse was heavily bet on* is possible in racing talk. The confidence sense does not: ✗ *it was not bet on by me* — say *I wouldn't bet on it*.

bind over.verb type: **action** — dynamic and telic, a court act with a result: the defendant is now held for trial. Legal register, and the perfect and past dominate: *the magistrate bound them over*.
bind over.passive: **yes**, and the passive is the ordinary form — *he was bound over on two felony counts*, *the case was bound over to the grand jury in March*.

bind up.verb type: **action** in sense 1 — dynamic and literary: *bind up the wound*. Senses 2 and 3 survive only as frozen passive participles behaving like adjectives: *bound up with*, *bound up in*.
bind up.passive: **yes** — *the wound was bound up before the doctor arrived*. Senses 2 and 3 exist in the passive alone: *her fate is bound up with his*, *he was bound up in the campaign*, with no active ✗ *the war bound up her fate with his*.

bite back.verb type: **action** — dynamic in both: suppressing a remark (sense 1) and retaliating (sense 2). Progressive is fine either way: *she was biting back a laugh*.
bite back.passive: **restricted** — sense 1 passivizes awkwardly: *the retort was bitten back* is grammatical but stilted. Sense 2 has no object and so no passive at all: ✗ *the market was bitten back by*.

bite into.verb type: **action** — dynamic in all three: sinking teeth in, costs eating away at profit, a strap cutting a shoulder. Progressive is normal: *the rope was biting into his hands*.
bite into.passive: **restricted** — the literal sense allows a prepositional passive in the perfect (*every cupcake had been bitten into*), and the money sense is heavy but attested: *profits were badly bitten into by fuel costs*. Avoid it with the cutting sense: ✗ *his shoulder was bitten into by the strap*.

bite off.verb type: **action** — dynamic and telic: *he bit off the cap and spat it out*. Sense 2 is the fixed idiom *bite off more than you can chew*, which resists any reshaping.
bite off.passive: **yes** in sense 1 — *the cap had been bitten off*, *two of the buttons were bitten off*. The idiom keeps its active shape: ✗ *more than he could chew was bitten off by him*.

bleed dry.verb type: **action** — dynamic and resultative: *dry* is a result predicate on the object, so the pattern is verb + object + complement (*bleed the company dry*), close to but not the same as a linking use.
bleed dry.passive: **yes** — *he has been bled dry by his own relatives*, *the treasury was bled dry by four years of war*. The complement *dry* travels with the verb.

bleed off.verb type: **action** — dynamic, deliberate, and gradual, which suits the progressive: *a leaky seal had been bleeding off coolant since spring*.
bleed off.passive: **yes** — *the pressure was bled off through a second line*, *cash was quietly bled off for two years*.

bleed out.verb type: **action** — dynamic in both: dying of blood loss (sense 1) and draining a line (sense 2). Progressive fits either: *he was bleeding out on the shoulder of the road*.
bleed out.passive: **yes** in sense 2 — *the brake lines were bled out before the test drive*. **No** in sense 1, which has no object: ✗ *he was bled out on the highway* means something else entirely.

blow away.verb type: **action** — dynamic in all four: wind carrying something off, astonishing someone, winning easily, shooting someone dead. Progressive is fine: *the tarp was blowing away*.
blow away.passive: **yes** — and in sense 2 the passive is the usual form: *I was blown away by the ending*. Also *the roof was blown away*, *they were blown away in the third quarter*, *he was blown away in the parking lot*.

blow in.verb type: **action** — dynamic, describing an arrival, usually a sudden or unannounced one: *he blew in around midnight with no luggage*.
blow in.passive: **no** — intransitive, so there is nothing to promote: ✗ *he was blown in at midnight* would mean the wind carried him.

blow off.verb type: **action** — dynamic in all four senses: skipping an obligation, brushing off a person, releasing tension (*blow off steam*), and tearing something loose.
blow off.passive: **yes** — *the meeting was blown off twice*, *I was blown off again*, *the roof was blown off in the storm*. The idiom resists it: ✗ *steam was blown off by him*.

blow out.verb type: **action** — dynamic throughout: extinguishing a flame, a tire bursting (sense 2, intransitive), wrecking a knee, winning by a wide margin.
blow out.passive: **yes** where there is an object — *the candles were blown out*, *his knee was blown out in the second half*, *they were blown out 42 to 3*. **No** for sense 2: ✗ *the tire was blown out by itself* — say *the tire blew out*.

blow over.verb type: action — dynamic throughout: the weather and scandal senses are intransitive happenings (*the storm blew over*), sense 3 is the causative counterpart (*the wind blew the fence over*). No stative or linking use.
blow over.passive: **yes** in the knock-down sense, where it is the commonest form — *the patio umbrella was blown over in the night*, *they were blown over like dominoes*. No passive of the intransitive senses: ✗ *the storm was blown over*, ✗ *it was blown over by the next news cycle*.

blow through.verb type: action — dynamic in all three senses, of spending, of moving fast, and of racing through work. No stative or linking use.
blow through.passive: **restricted** — a prepositional passive is possible in the spending sense (*the advance was blown through in four months*) but sounds odd, and the active is standard. The movement senses have none: ✗ *the stop sign was blown through by the driver*.

blow up.verb type: action — dynamic in every sense, whether the thing explodes on its own (sense 1, intransitive) or somebody explodes it (sense 1, transitive). Senses 3, 5, and 6 — losing your temper, becoming famous, getting out of hand — are dynamic intransitives; none of the senses is stative or linking.
blow up.passive: **yes** in the transitive senses — *the old span was blown up on a Sunday*, *the air mattress had already been blown up*, *blow the frame up* → *the frame was blown up until you could read the plate*. No passive of the intransitive senses: ✗ *the transformer was blown up at two in the morning* (in the 'it exploded' reading), ✗ *the song was blown up over one weekend*.

break away.verb type: action — dynamic in all three senses: pulling free, splitting off, and pulling ahead in a race. No stative or linking use; the noun *breakaway* comes from sense 3.
break away.passive: **no** — intransitive in every sense, so there is nothing to promote: ✗ *the crowd was broken away from*, ✗ *the union was broken away from by a dozen members*. What you leave rides on *from*, and that phrase does not passivize.

break down.verb type: action — dynamic throughout, both in the intransitive happenings (*the van broke down*, *she broke down on the stand*, *negotiations broke down*) and in the transitive acts (*break down the estimate*, *break down the door*). No stative or linking use.
break down.passive: **yes** in the transitive senses — *the numbers were broken down by region*, *the door was broken down by firefighters*. No passive of the intransitive senses: ✗ *the van was broken down outside Amarillo* (that is the adjective, not the passive), ✗ *negotiations were broken down after two days*.

break even.verb type: action — dynamic, an achievement verb: reaching the point where income matches outlay. *Even* is a frozen resultative complement, so the phrase has the shape of a linking pattern (compare *run dry*, *fall flat*), but nothing may be substituted for it. The progressive is fine: *we're breaking even this month*.
break even.passive: **no** — the phrase takes no object at all, so there is nothing to make the subject: ✗ *even was broken by the restaurant*, ✗ *the trip will be broken even on*. The idea goes into the noun instead: *the break-even point*.

break in.verb type: action — dynamic in every sense — forcing entry, wearing gear in, training a new hire, and interrupting. No stative or linking use; the noun is a *break-in*.
break in.passive: **restricted** — natural in the wear-in/train-in sense: *the boots were broken in before the hike*, *new catchers are broken in slowly*. The burglary sense is intransitive and has no passive (✗ *the house was broken in* — say *broken into*), and the interrupting sense passivizes only marginally: ?*the call was broken in on*.

break into.verb type: action — dynamic in all four senses, from forcing entry to suddenly starting a canter, a sweat, or applause. No stative or linking use.
break into.passive: **yes** in sense 1, where the prepositional passive is entirely ordinary — *his car has been broken into twice this year*, *the shed was broken into over the weekend*. The other senses do not passivize: ✗ *a canter was broken into by the horse*, ✗ *television was broken into by her*, ✗ *the emergency water was broken into* is at best marginal.

break off.verb type: action — dynamic in every sense, and sense 1 works both ways: somebody breaks a piece off, or the piece breaks off by itself. No stative or linking use.
break off.passive: **yes** in the transitive senses — *negotiations were broken off after two days*, *the engagement was broken off in April*, *a corner had been broken off*. No passive when nothing does the breaking (✗ *the handle was broken off in my hand* in the intransitive reading — that is the adjective) or in the stop-speaking sense.

break out.verb type: action — dynamic throughout: fires and fights start (sense 1), prisoners escape (sense 2), a rash appears (sense 3), and somebody produces the good glasses (sense 4) or itemizes the costs (sense 5). No stative or linking use; the nouns are an *outbreak* and a *breakout*.
break out.passive: **restricted** — fine in the two transitive senses: *the sparklers were broken out at dusk*, *the costs were broken out by department*. No passive of senses 1–3, which take no object: ✗ *a fire was broken out in the kitchen*, ✗ *hives were broken out in by him*.

break out of.verb type: action — dynamic in both senses, escaping a place and escaping a pattern. No stative or linking use.
break out of.passive: **restricted** — only the *break somebody out of somewhere* pattern passivizes: *he was broken out of a federal facility by two accomplices*. The ordinary escape and pattern senses do not: ✗ *the county jail was broken out of*, ✗ *the slump can't be broken out of*.

break through.verb type: action — dynamic in all three senses, of forcing a way through a barrier, of a decisive advance, and of reaching somebody emotionally. No stative or linking use; the noun is a *breakthrough*.
break through.passive: **restricted** — the prepositional passive is possible in sense 1 but stiff: *the barricade was finally broken through*; most writers keep the active. Senses 2 and 3 take no object and have no passive at all: ✗ *the third try was broken through on*.

break up.verb type: action — dynamic in every sense, from ending a relationship to dispersing a crowd to a signal cutting in and out. No stative or linking use; note that *broken up* in *he was pretty broken up about it* is an adjective (upset), not this passive.
break up.passive: **yes** in the transitive senses — *the crowd was broken up by police*, *the estate was broken up into six lots*, *the fight was broken up before anyone got hurt*. No passive of the intransitive senses: ✗ *they were broken up after four years* in the relationship reading, ✗ *you were broken up on the call*.

break with.verb type: action — dynamic: an act of ending an association, not a state of being apart. No stative or linking use; the progressive is fine (*he is breaking with the party on this*).
break with.passive: **restricted** — the prepositional passive is grammatical but stilted, and formal writing tends to recast: ?*a century of practice was broken with*, ?*the old formula had been broken with*. The active is the normal form: *the design breaks with a century of practice*.

bring about.verb type: action — dynamic and causative: making something happen. No stative or linking use, though it takes abstract subjects freely (*the strike brought about the contract*).
bring about.passive: **yes**, and the passive is one of its commonest shapes in formal writing — *the reforms were brought about by pressure from below*, *the change was brought about faster by the lawsuit than by anything else*.

bring along.verb type: action — dynamic in both senses: carrying somebody or something with you, and developing a rookie or a crop. No stative or linking use.
bring along.passive: **restricted** — natural in the develop sense: *the rookie is being brought along slowly*, *the tomatoes were brought along by the warm weather*. Grammatical but uncommon in sense 1, where the active or an imperative is normal: ?*a jacket should be brought along*.

bring around.verb type: action — dynamic in all three senses — reviving somebody, winning somebody over, and delivering something to a place. No stative or linking use.
bring around.passive: **yes** — *he was brought around with smelling salts*, *the committee was brought around once they saw the numbers*, *the trailer was brought around at eight*.

bring back.verb type: action — dynamic in every sense: returning a thing, reinstating a practice, and triggering a memory. No stative or linking use; the memory sense takes an inanimate subject (*that smell brings back my grandmother's kitchen*) but is still dynamic.
bring back.passive: **yes** in senses 1 and 2 — *the drill was never brought back*, *the tax was brought back by two states*, *the old logo was brought back after the backlash*. The memory sense passivizes stiffly: ?*it was all brought back by the photos*; the active is normal.

bring down.verb type: action — dynamic and causative in all three senses: toppling something, reducing a number, and depressing somebody. No stative or linking use.
bring down.passive: **yes** — *the mayor was brought down by one reporter*, *the helicopter was brought down by ground fire*, *inflation has to be brought down*. Sense 3 works too, usually with *get*: *don't get brought down by one bad review*.

bring forward.verb type: action — dynamic in all three senses: rescheduling earlier, proposing, and carrying a figure over. No stative or linking use.
bring forward.passive: **yes**, and it is the usual form in the scheduling and bookkeeping senses — *the hearing was brought forward by two weeks*, *an amendment nobody had read was brought forward*, *the balance brought forward from last quarter*.

bring in.verb type: action — dynamic in all four senses: introducing a rule, earning money, summoning somebody, and returning a verdict. No stative or linking use.
bring in.passive: **yes** in senses 1, 3, and 4 — *a curfew was brought in after the second fire*, *he was brought in for questioning*, *a verdict of not guilty was brought in*. The earning sense resists it, as measure-like objects usually do: ✗ *nine thousand a month is brought in by the shop*.

bring off.verb type: action — dynamic: succeeding at something difficult, an achievement verb. No stative or linking use.
bring off.passive: **restricted** — grammatical (*the upset was brought off on the road*, *a live broadcast from the site had never been brought off before*) but the active dominates, and American speech reaches for *pulled off* instead.

bring on.verb type: action — dynamic in every sense: triggering something, hiring somebody, and the frozen challenge *bring it on*. No stative or linking use.
bring on.passive: **yes** in senses 1 and 2 — *the migraine was brought on by stress*, *two more engineers were brought on in March*, *she was brought on as a contractor first*. The challenge is frozen with *it* and has no passive: ✗ *it was brought on*.

bring out.verb type: action — dynamic in all four senses: releasing a product, making a quality noticeable, drawing something out of a person, and carrying something out for use. No stative or linking use.
bring out.passive: **yes** — *a new edition is brought out every fall*, *it was brought out on vinyl first*, *the folding chairs were brought out before dark*. Sense 2 passivizes but sounds stiff: ?*the sweetness is brought out by salt*.

bring to.verb type: action — dynamic: restoring somebody to consciousness, an achievement verb with a fixed adverbial *to*. No stative or linking use.
bring to.passive: **restricted** — the passive exists (*she was brought to by cold water*, *the driver was brought to at the scene*) but is uncommon; because the object must sit in the middle in the active, the passive strands *to* and sounds stilted to many speakers, who say *was revived* instead.

bring up.verb type: action — dynamic in all four senses: raising a child, mentioning a subject, displaying something on screen, and vomiting. No stative or linking use.
bring up.passive: **yes**, and sense 1 lives mainly in the passive — *she was brought up by her grandparents*, *he was brought up on a farm*. Also *the divorce was brought up twice at dinner*, *the invoice was brought up on the big monitor*.

build in.verb type: action — dynamic: making something a permanent part of a plan or a structure from the start. No stative or linking use, though the participle shades into an adjective (*built-in shelves*).
build in.passive: **yes**, and it is very common — *a penalty for late delivery is built in*, *the shelves are built in, so they stay with the house*, *a two-percent raise was built in from the first year*.

build into.verb type: action — dynamic: making something a permanent part of a named larger thing. No stative or linking use; the resulting participle behaves adjectivally (*the fee is built into the price*).
build into.passive: **yes**, and the passive is the commonest form — *the penalty is built into the lease*, *redundancy was built into the system after the outage*, *an error had been built into the formula years earlier*.

build on.verb type: action — dynamic in both senses: using something as a foundation, and adding a structure to a building. No stative or linking use.
build on.passive: **restricted** — sense 1 passivizes freely as a participle (*a career built on one lucky year*, *the method was built on what the last team learned*), but a full agentive passive is awkward: ?*the first album was built on by the second*. Sense 2 is fine: *the porch was built on in the eighties*.

build up.verb type: action — dynamic in every sense: accumulating, strengthening, and hyping. No stative or linking use; the noun is a *buildup* and *built-up* is a separate adjective.
build up.passive: **yes** in the transitive senses — *her mileage is being built up before the race*, *his confidence was built up over two years of therapy*, *the sequel was built up so much that it couldn't win*. No passive of the accumulating sense: ✗ *sediment is built up behind the dam by the river*.

burn down.verb type: action — dynamic, and it works both ways: somebody burns the building down, or the building burns down by itself. No stative or linking use.
burn down.passive: **yes** in the transitive sense — *the old depot was burned down by vandals*, *the whole block was burned down in one night*. No passive when the building is the subject: ✗ *the church was burned down in 1908* is the causative reading only, not the intransitive one.

burn off.verb type: action — dynamic in all three senses: using up energy, removing something by burning, and fog clearing. No stative or linking use.
burn off.passive: **yes** in senses 1 and 2 — *the underbrush was burned off before the dry season*, *about four hundred calories are burned off on a four-mile walk*, *the paint was burned off rather than scraped*. No passive of the fog sense, which takes no object: ✗ *the fog is burned off by ten*.

burn out.verb type: action — dynamic in every sense: failing from heat, exhausting somebody, a fire dying, and losing a home to fire. No stative or linking use; *burned out* as in *he looks burned out* is the adjective.
burn out.passive: **yes** in the transitive senses, and sense 4 is almost only passive — *four families were burned out of the building*; also *the motor was burned out in a week*, and with *get* in the exhaustion sense: *half the residents get burned out before their third year*. No passive of the intransitive senses: ✗ *the starter was burned out twice* (as an event), ✗ *the fire was burned out by dawn*.

burn through.verb type: action — dynamic in all three senses: using something up fast, making a hole, and racing through work. No stative or linking use.
burn through.passive: **restricted** — best in the literal sense, where it is common: *the tarp had been burned through*, *two layers of glove were burned through*. The money and work senses passivize awkwardly and are usually left active: ?*the seed money was burned through in nine months*.

burn up.verb type: action — dynamic in every sense. The fever sense is dynamic but locked in the progressive (*the kid is burning up*, not ✗ *the kid burns up* in that reading); the anger sense takes an inanimate subject and a frozen middle object.
burn up.passive: **yes** in sense 1 — *every letter was burned up in the fireplace*, *the papers had all been burned up*. **No** in the anger sense, where the object never leaves the middle: ✗ *I was burned up by it that nobody called* (*I was burned up about it* is the adjective). The reentry, fever, and distance uses are intransitive and have no passive.

burst in.verb type: action — dynamic: entering suddenly, or interrupting. No stative or linking use.
burst in.passive: **no** — intransitive in both senses, so there is nothing to promote: ✗ *the room was burst in*. Even the prepositional *burst in on* barely passivizes: ?*our meeting was burst in on*, which most speakers would recast.

burst into.verb type: action — dynamic in all three senses: rushing into a place, suddenly crying or laughing, and catching fire. No stative or linking use.
burst into.passive: **no** — the prepositional passive fails across the board: ✗ *the office was burst into*, ✗ *the apartment was burst into by agents*. In senses 2 and 3 the noun after *into* is part of a frozen phrase (*tears*, *laughter*, *flames*) and can never become a subject: ✗ *tears were burst into*.

burst out.verb type: action — dynamic in all three senses: starting to laugh or cry, blurting something out, and rushing out of a place. No stative or linking use.
burst out.passive: **no** — intransitive throughout, with no object anywhere: ✗ *laughing was burst out*, ✗ *the building was burst out of*. Even the quoted-speech sense (*"That's a lie," he burst out*) has no object to promote.

bust in.verb type: action — dynamic: forcing your way in, or barging into a conversation. Informal American; no stative or linking use.
bust in.passive: **no** — intransitive in both senses: ✗ *the back door was busted in* is a different, literal verb (busting a door), not this one, and ✗ *the conversation was busted in on* is not idiomatic.

bust out.verb type: action — dynamic in all three senses: escaping, producing something for use, and starting to laugh. Informal; no stative or linking use.
bust out.passive: **restricted** — fine in the transitive senses: *the karaoke machine was busted out at midnight*, *he was busted out of a federal facility a week later*. No passive when the escaper is the subject or in the laughing sense: ✗ *the county jail was busted out of*, ✗ *laughing was busted out*.

bust up.verb type: action — dynamic in all three senses: breaking up a fight, wrecking something, and a couple splitting. Informal; no stative or linking use.
bust up.passive: **yes** in senses 1 and 2, and the informal *get*-passive is the natural form — *the fight was busted up by the bouncers*, *the truck got busted up on a gravel road*, *her knee got busted up skiing*. No passive of the couple sense: ✗ *they were busted up in the spring*.

buy back.verb type: action — dynamic: repurchasing what you sold. No stative or linking use; the noun is a *buyback*.
buy back.passive: **yes**, and it is standard in business writing — *four million shares were bought back last quarter*, *the ring was bought back a year later*, *the lease can be bought back if the mileage is low*.

buy in.verb type: action — dynamic in both senses: purchasing a stake, and getting behind an idea. No stative or linking use — even the agreement sense describes coming around, not being in a state.
buy in.passive: **no** — it takes no object at all, so there is nothing to promote: ✗ *the plan was bought in*, ✗ *the policy hasn't been bought in yet*. English puts the idea in the noun instead: *we need staff buy-in*.

buy into.verb type: action — dynamic in both senses: accepting an idea and purchasing a stake. No stative or linking use, though sense 1 often appears in the perfect describing a settled belief (*he has bought into the theory*).
buy into.passive: **restricted** — the prepositional passive is marginal and mostly avoided: ?*the theory has been widely bought into*, ✗ *the whole story was never bought into by me*. The stake sense does not passivize at all: ✗ *the practice was bought into in 2016*.

buy off.verb type: action — dynamic: paying somebody to stop opposing you. No stative or linking use.
buy off.passive: **yes**, and the passive is common because the payer is often unknown — *the witnesses were bought off long before the trial*, *the inspector had been bought off*, *they were bought off with a consulting contract*.

buy out.verb type: action — dynamic: purchasing somebody's whole share, or paying to end a contract. No stative or linking use; the noun is a *buyout*.
buy out.passive: **yes** — *he was bought out by his brother in 2019*, *the whole chain was bought out by a private equity firm*, *the last year of his contract was bought out*.

buy up.verb type: action — dynamic: purchasing all of something available. No stative or linking use.
buy up.passive: **yes** — *half the block was bought up in two years*, *every generator in the county had been bought up*, *the whole print run was bought up by one buyer*.
